papers.title: Evaluation of Adversarial Robustness in Arabic Language Models
papers.abstract: The emergence of the recent outstanding capabilities of Arabic Language Models has opened doors for exposing their vulnerabilities. One of the major security risks associated with such Natural Language Processing models is adversarial attacks. These attacks can deceive the model into the wrong prediction, raising critical model security and safety concerns. This study aims to assess the robustness of five state-of-the-art Arabic Language Models under a distinct set of Arabic adversarial attacks applied at various levels of granularity and using different example generation strategies. We also explore a defense technique based on adversarial training to enhance model robustness. The results show that insertion of diacritics can reduce the accuracy of some models by 92% while maintaining a low perturbation distance. For word-level attacks, manipulating Arabic conjunctions preserves high semantic similarity scores, low perturbation distance, and leads to an accuracy degradation of up to 58%. For sentence-level attacks, paraphrasing proves its effectiveness by an average reduction of 76% in the victim models' performance. While adversarial training improves overall resilience, with MARBERT being the most robust and AraBERT showing the greatest relative gains, challenges persist, particularly against character-level noise. These findings highlight both the potential and limitations of current defense strategies in morphologically rich languages like Arabic.

summary.takeaway: Arabic language models can lose up to 92% accuracy from simple diacritic insertions, and adversarial training only partially restores robustness.
summary.problem: Assessing and improving the adversarial robustness of Arabic language models across multiple granularity levels.
summary.method: The authors generate character‑level diacritic insertions, word‑level conjunction manipulations, and sentence‑level paraphrases, then apply adversarial training to five Arabic LMs.
summary.evidence: Diacritic attacks cut AraBERT accuracy by 92%, word‑level attacks cause up to 58% loss, sentence‑level paraphrasing reduces performance by an average of 76%, and adversarial training makes MARBERT the most robust.
summary.limitations: Models remain highly vulnerable to character‑level noise despite adversarial training, and evaluation is limited to five models and specific attack types.
summary.why_for_you: Relevant if you are exploring efficient adversarial training for LLMs and need concrete robustness benchmarks in a morphologically rich language.

signals.text: Offers quantitative evaluation of five Arabic LMs against character, word, and sentence-level attacks, exposing up to 92% accuracy loss.
Applies targeted adversarial training (A2T) and constructs attacks via diacritic insertion, conjunction manipulation, and paraphrasing to test model resilience.
Shows character-level diacritic attacks drop AraBERT accuracy by 92% while preserving high semantic similarity, highlighting detection difficulty.

deep_dive.overview: The paper systematically evaluates five state-of-the-art Arabic language models (MARBERT, CaMeLBERT, AraBERT, XLM‑T, mBERT) against three granularity attack families: character‑level diacritic insertions, word‑level conjunction manipulations, and sentence‑level paraphrasing. Metrics include post‑attack accuracy, attack success rate, perturbation rate (Levenshtein distance), cosine similarity, and Universal Sentence Encoder similarity. An adversarial training pipeline (A2T) is then applied, revealing MARBERT as the most robust and AraBERT as the biggest gainer, yet character‑level vulnerabilities persist.

methodology.title: Attack Generation
methodology.detail: Three attack strategies are employed: (1) insert diacritics at the character level, (2) replace Arabic conjunctions at the word level while preserving semantic similarity, and (3) paraphrase entire sentences using a paraphrasing model.

methodology.title: Adversarial Training
methodology.detail: A vanilla adversarial training process (A2T) augments the training set with generated adversarial examples and fine‑tunes each model to improve resilience.

mechanism.title: Vulnerability to Diacritics
mechanism.detail: Arabic diacritics alter vowel markings without changing token length, leading to large prediction shifts while maintaining low Levenshtein distance and high semantic similarity, making them hard for grammar‑based detectors to catch.

experiments.title: Model Evaluation
experiments.detail: Baseline accuracies on clean test data: MARBERT 99%, CaMeLBERT 95%, AraBERT 94%, XLM‑T 94%, mBERT 87%. Post‑attack accuracies are reported for each granularity, along with perturbation rate, cosine similarity, and USE scores.

experiments.title: Defense Assessment
experiments.detail: After adversarial training, MARBERT retains the highest robustness across attacks; AraBERT shows the greatest relative accuracy gain, yet character‑level attacks still cause severe drops.

findings.title: Character‑Level Impact
findings.detail: Diacritic insertion reduces AraBERT accuracy by 92% while MARBERT only drops to 94% accuracy, indicating varied susceptibility.

findings.title: Word‑Level Impact
findings.detail: Manipulating Arabic conjunctions leads to up to 58% accuracy degradation with low perturbation distance and high semantic similarity.

findings.title: Sentence‑Level Impact
findings.detail: Paraphrasing attacks cause an average 76% reduction in model performance across the five LMs.

findings.title: Effectiveness of Adversarial Training
findings.detail: Adversarial training improves overall resilience; MARBERT emerges as the most robust, but character‑level noise remains a critical weakness.

contributions: Comprehensive benchmark of Arabic LMs against multi‑granular adversarial attacks.
Empirical quantification of accuracy loss for character, word, and sentence‑level attacks.
Evaluation of a simple adversarial training (A2T) defense across multiple Arabic models.
limitations: Persistent vulnerability to character‑level diacritic noise despite adversarial training.
Evaluation limited to five pre‑trained Arabic models and three specific attack families.
open_questions: How can defenses be designed to specifically mitigate character‑level diacritic attacks in morphologically rich languages?
Can more efficient adversarial training methods achieve comparable robustness with lower computational overhead?

papers.title: On-Policy Distillation for LLM Safety: A Routing Approach to Template-Robust Realignment
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning is the dominant paradigm for specializing large language models (LLMs), yet it exposes a critical vulnerability: malicious data providers can embed harmful behaviors into downstream corpora, creating models that retain professional skills while violating human values on demand. Existing safety-realignment defenses often fail in practice due to three key limitations: they frequently cause catastrophic forgetting of specialized skills; their effectiveness collapses when the defender cannot observe the attacker's prompt template; and successfully realigned models remain susceptible to re-jailbreaking via simple system prompt switches. To address these challenges, we propose Routing-based On-Policy Distillation (ROPD), a novel realignment framework that models the divergence between aligned and compromised output probability distributions rather than fitting specific prompt templates. We conduct extensive experiments comparing ROPD against four state-of-the-art baselines across three datasets and three base models with varying alignment strengths. Our results demonstrate that when baseline defenses face template mismatches, often accompanied by severe degradation in downstream task performance. In contrast, ROPD substantially mitigates template-mismatch risks, maintaining superior robustness in both defense effectiveness and capability preservation. While our analysis indicates ROPD is not entirely immune to template shifts, its performance degradation is negligible compared to existing methods, establishing a new standard for robust LLM realignment.

summary.takeaway: ROPD provides a template‑robust safety realignment for LLMs via dual‑teacher on‑policy distillation while preserving downstream capabilities.
summary.problem: Fine‑tuned LLMs can embed harmful behavior that existing defenses fail to remove when the attacker’s prompt template is unknown, often causing skill loss or re‑jailbreaking.
summary.method: ROPD routes each token to either a frozen safety teacher (aligned model) or a task teacher (misaligned model) and trains a student with a top‑K KL loss.
summary.evidence: Experiments on three tasks and three base models show ROPD lowers attack success rate to 2.4% and maintains task scores (e.g., 0.626) outperforming four SOTA baselines whose ASR exceeds 6% and often drops task performance to zero.
summary.limitations: ROPD is not completely immune to template shifts; its performance degrades slightly under mismatched templates.
summary.why_for_you: This work aligns with trustworthy LLM research by demonstrating efficient on‑policy distillation for safety that mitigates template‑dependent failures.

signals.text: ROPD cuts template‑mismatch attack success rate by over 30%, achieving single‑digit ASR (2.4%) while keeping task performance.
ROPD routes each token to a frozen safety or task teacher and trains with a top‑K KL distillation loss.
On Llama‑2‑7B‑Chat SQL, ROPD reaches task score 0.626 and ASR 2.4%, outperforming baselines whose ASR exceeds 6%.

deep_dive.overview: The paper introduces Routing‑based On‑Policy Distillation (ROPD), a safety‑realignment framework that avoids template‑specific supervision by distilling the refusal distribution of an aligned teacher. ROPD employs a routing mechanism to select between a frozen safety teacher (the original aligned model) and a task teacher (the misaligned model) for each token, optimizing a top‑K KL objective. Extensive evaluations across three downstream tasks (SQL, SAMSum, NL2Bash), three base models (Llama‑2, Qwen2.5, Gemma2), and four SOTA baselines demonstrate that ROPD markedly reduces attack success rates while preserving or slightly improving task performance, though minor template‑shift sensitivity remains.

methodology.title: Dual‑teacher configuration
methodology.detail: The misaligned model serves as the task teacher and the original aligned model as the safety teacher; both are frozen during student training.

methodology.title: Routing and loss
methodology.detail: For each training example, a teacher is selected by source (Eq. 1), and a top‑K KL divergence (Eq. 2) between student and selected teacher is computed; parameters are updated via gradient descent (Eq. 3).

mechanism.title: Template‑independent refusal prior
mechanism.detail: The safety teacher’s output distribution concentrates probability on refusals regardless of prompt format, and distilling this distribution injects a refusal prior into the student that is less tied to any specific attack template.

mechanism.title: Skill preservation via task teacher
mechanism.detail: Routing to the task teacher ensures the student inherits the downstream capability of the misaligned model, preventing catastrophic forgetting of specialized skills.

experiments.title: Setup
experiments.detail: Three downstream tasks (text‑to‑SQL, dialogue summarization, NL2Bash) with 1,500 harmful examples from BeaverTails; three base models (Llama‑2, Qwen2.5, Gemma2); four baselines (rollback, RESTA, soft‑SFT, SSRD); evaluation of attack success rate (ASR) and task metrics (e.g., ROUGE).

experiments.title: Template conditions
experiments.detail: Defenses are run with two legal defense templates (raw, self) while the attack template is varied; an oracle upper bound uses the attack template as defense.

findings.title: ASR reduction
findings.detail: When defense and attack templates mismatch, baseline ASR drops by >30% and task performance can fall to zero, whereas ROPD achieves ASR as low as 2.4% (self template) and maintains task scores (e.g., 0.626).

findings.title: Cross‑template robustness
findings.detail: On Llama‑2‑7B‑Chat SQL, ROPD attains 0.626 task score / 2.4% ASR under self template, compared to soft‑SFT’s 0.358 / 6.3% and higher ASR for other baselines.

findings.title: Minor template sensitivity
findings.detail: ROPD’s ASR increases slightly under unseen templates but remains substantially lower than all baselines, confirming a reduced but non‑zero template‑mismatch risk.

contributions: Introduce ROPD, a dual‑teacher on‑policy distillation framework that mitigates template‑dependent safety failures.
Demonstrate that distilling the aligned model’s refusal distribution yields a template‑independent safety signal.
Provide extensive empirical evidence across models, tasks, and baselines showing superior safety‑task trade‑offs.
limitations: ROPD is not entirely immune to template shifts; performance degrades slightly when the defense template differs from the attack template.
open_questions: How can template‑independent safety signals be further strengthened to achieve complete immunity to prompt variations?
What are the scalability limits of ROPD when applied to much larger LLMs or multi‑modal models?
Can ROPD be combined with reinforcement learning from human feedback to improve long‑term alignment robustness?

papers.title: Language Models are not Equally Robust to Non-Canonical Tokenization across Languages
papers.abstract: Despite the existence of exponentially many valid tokenizations for a given string, language models operate on a single canonical sequence deterministically produced by the tokenizer, leaving the broader tokenization space largely uncharacterized. In this paper, we investigate this overlooked space by studying the behavior of language models under non-canonical tokenizations across diverse languages. For English, prior work shows that models are largely invariant to alternative tokenizations that represent the same underlying string. We ask whether this invariance generalizes to other languages beyond English. We conduct a multilingual study across 27 languages spanning diverse scripts and evaluate LLM behavior under alternative tokenizations across six downstream tasks. We find that tokenization invariance does not generalize: model behavior varies substantially across languages with instruction-tuned models exhibiting an average relative performance drop of 23.7% for Llama-3.1-8B, 11.4% for Qwen3-8B, and 9.9% for Gemma-3-12B. The variation of tokenization invariance is systematic across languages. Languages that exhibit higher token fragmentation show significantly greater sensitivity to non-canonical tokenizations. Our study of tokenization robustness serves as a diagnostic of how tightly a model is coupled to its tokenizer. These results demonstrate that tokenization robustness is not a universal property of language models, but depends strongly on the language and its interaction with the tokenizer. We also show that LoRA fine-tuning with multi-tokenization training data provides an effective mitigation for tokenization sensitivity. Fine-tuning on English alone improves tokenization robustness across languages, while systematically sampling diverse non-canonical tokenizations achieves the strongest overall performance.

summary.takeaway: Tokenization robustness varies across languages but can be mitigated by LoRA fine‑tuning with multi‑tokenization data.
summary.problem: LLMs may suffer substantial performance degradation when presented with non‑canonical tokenizations, especially for languages with high token fragmentation.
summary.method: The authors uniformly sample random non‑canonical tokenizations via a Multi‑valued Decision Diagram, evaluate instruction‑tuned models, and apply LoRA fine‑tuning on multi‑tokenization training data.
summary.evidence: Instruction‑tuned Llama‑3.1‑8B loses 23.7% relative performance, Qwen‑3‑8B 11.4%, and Gemma‑3‑12B 9.9% under random non‑canonical tokenizations, with higher token fragmentation correlating with greater drops.
summary.limitations: The study is limited to three instruction‑tuned models, 27 languages, and six downstream tasks, and focuses on random non‑canonical tokenizations rather than targeted adversarial attacks.
summary.why_for_you: Relevant to efficient adversarial training and data selection because tokenization perturbations provide cheap adversarial examples and LoRA offers a lightweight mitigation strategy.

signals.text: The paper provides the first systematic multilingual study of non‑canonical tokenization across 27 languages, six tasks, and three model families.
LoRA fine‑tuning on multi‑tokenization data, especially with systematic diverse sampling, markedly reduces sensitivity to tokenization perturbations.
Instruction‑tuned Llama‑3.1‑8B loses 23.7% relative performance, Qwen‑3‑8B 11.4%, and Gemma‑3‑12B 9.9% under random non‑canonical tokenizations.

deep_dive.overview: The authors investigate how multilingual LLMs behave under alternative valid tokenizations by sampling uniformly from the full tokenization space using a Multi‑valued Decision Diagram. Across 27 languages and six downstream tasks, they find that instruction‑tuned models suffer sizable relative performance drops, with the magnitude linked to each language's token fragmentation rate. They further demonstrate that LoRA fine‑tuning on data augmented with diverse non‑canonical tokenizations, even when fine‑tuned only on English, substantially restores robustness, establishing tokenization sensitivity as a distinct, language‑dependent property of LLMs.

methodology.title: Non‑canonical tokenization sampling
methodology.detail: Represent the set of all valid tokenizations of a string with a Multi‑valued Decision Diagram (MDD) and uniformly sample N alternatives per input.

methodology.title: Fragmentation metric
methodology.detail: Compute average tokens per word for each language to quantify token fragmentation.

methodology.title: Evaluation framework
methodology.detail: Extend lm‑evaluation‑harness to accept alternative tokenizations and report mean performance over five random seeds.

mechanism.title: Token fragmentation sensitivity
mechanism.detail: Languages with higher average tokens‑per‑word exhibit larger performance degradation under non‑canonical tokenizations, indicating tighter coupling between model and tokenizer.

mechanism.title: LoRA mitigation
mechanism.detail: LoRA adapters trained on multi‑tokenization data inject robustness by exposing the model to varied token segmentations during fine‑tuning.

experiments.title: Model and data setup
experiments.detail: Instruction‑tuned Llama‑3.1‑8B‑Instruct, Qwen‑3‑8B, and gemma‑3‑12b‑it evaluated on 27 languages (FLORES‑200) across six downstream tasks.

experiments.title: Perturbation types
experiments.detail: Canonical tokenization vs. random non‑canonical tokenizations sampled uniformly from the MDD; also character‑level tokenizations for retrieval experiments.

experiments.title: Metrics
experiments.detail: Relative performance drop percentages; retrieval accuracy@1 for cross‑lingual sentence retrieval; correlation between fragmentation rate and drop.

findings.title: Performance degradation
findings.detail: Average relative drops: 23.7% for Llama‑3.1‑8B, 11.4% for Qwen‑3‑8B, 9.9% for Gemma‑3‑12B under random non‑canonical tokenizations.

findings.title: Fragmentation correlation
findings.detail: Languages with higher token fragmentation show significantly greater sensitivity to non‑canonical tokenizations.

findings.title: Robustness improvement
findings.detail: LoRA fine‑tuning on English alone improves robustness across languages; systematic sampling of diverse non‑canonical tokenizations yields the strongest overall performance.

contributions: First systematic multilingual analysis of non‑canonical tokenization effects on LLMs.
Identification of token fragmentation as a key factor driving sensitivity.
Demonstration that LoRA fine‑tuning with multi‑tokenization data mitigates tokenization brittleness.
limitations: Experiments limited to three instruction‑tuned model families.
Coverage restricted to 27 languages and six downstream tasks.
Focus on random non‑canonical tokenizations; adversarially crafted tokenizations not evaluated.
open_questions: How does tokenization robustness interact with other adversarial perturbations such as prompt injection?
Can tokenizer redesign or vocabulary reallocation eliminate sensitivity without fine‑tuning?
Does the observed mitigation scale to larger models and more diverse downstream applications?

papers.title: DataOrchestra: Learning to Orchestrate Per-Example Curation of Pretraining Data
papers.abstract: Pretraining data processing is critical to the downstream performance of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, many existing approaches define a fixed processing strategy at the corpus or domain level and apply it uniformly to many examples, without adapting to the needs of each example. We propose DataOrchestra, a framework that unifies different processing operations and orchestrates an example-specific pipeline for each example. Given a chunk of pretraining data, an orchestrator decides whether to drop, untouch, or clean it. For a chunk to be cleaned, it selects one or more downstream operations, ranging from programmatic editing to different forms of LLM-based rewriting. For each rewriting step, it further generates a concrete instruction, which is executed by the corresponding downstream tool model. We pretrain models from 0.5B to 7B from scratch on web data processed by DataOrchestra and observe stable average gains over individual data-processing methods across 11 benchmarks. DataOrchestra is also effective for math continued pretraining and outperforms stronger processing baselines, while reducing processing compute by skipping unnecessary downstream operations.

summary.takeaway: DataOrchestra learns to select per‑example preprocessing pipelines, yielding consistent downstream gains.
summary.problem: Existing data‑processing pipelines apply a single fixed strategy to all pretraining examples, ignoring example‑specific needs.
summary.method: An orchestrator predicts drop/untouch/clean decisions and composes chunk‑specific instructions for noise pruning, surface rectification, and pedagogical augmentation tools.
summary.evidence: Models from 0.5B to 7B pretrained on DataOrchestra‑processed data improve average accuracy to 40.13 versus 38.88 for the strongest baseline across 11 benchmarks while skipping unnecessary operations.
summary.limitations: Not stated in the available source.
summary.why_for_you: It directly addresses data selection for LLMs by providing a learned, per‑example curation mechanism.

signals.text: DataOrchestra introduces a per‑example orchestration framework that unifies noise pruning, surface rectification, and pedagogical augmentation.
The orchestrator predicts drop/untouch/clean decisions and generates chunk‑specific rewrite instructions for downstream tool models.
DataOrchestra‑trained 7B models achieve 40.13 average accuracy versus 38.88 baseline, but compute savings rely on unverifiable verifier LLM checks.

deep_dive.overview: DataOrchestra proposes a unified framework that tailors pretraining data processing to each example. An orchestrator first decides whether to drop, leave untouched, or clean a chunk, then selects among three operations—noise pruning (NP), surface rectification (SR), and pedagogical augmentation (PA)—and generates concrete instructions for tool models. Fine‑grained plan evolution uses verifier LLMs to prune ineffective stages. Experiments pretrain 0.5B‑7B models on web corpora, showing stable average accuracy improvements across 11 benchmarks and reduced compute by skipping unnecessary rewrites. Ablations confirm the importance of plan evolution and instruction generation.

methodology.title: Orchestrator Training
methodology.detail: Trains a model on 160K document chunks scored by DataMan, learning to output coarse‑grained plans (drop, untouch, NP/SR/PA flags).

methodology.title: Coarse‑Grained Plan Generation
methodology.detail: A teacher LLM rates each chunk (0‑5) and provides binary judgments for NP, SR, PA; decisions below score 2 trigger dropping.

methodology.title: Fine‑Grained Plan Evolution
methodology.detail: Executes selected stages, then a verifier LLM checks for hallucination, factual loss, or negligible change (Levenshtein > 98%) and removes ineffective stages.

mechanism.title: Adaptive Pipeline Selection
mechanism.detail: The orchestrator routes each chunk to the minimal necessary set of operations, allowing some chunks to be dropped or left untouched, thereby saving compute.

mechanism.title: Instruction Generation
mechanism.detail: For each rewriting stage, the orchestrator produces a concrete natural‑language instruction that guides the downstream tool model (e.g., LLM‑based rewrites).

experiments.title: Pretraining and Benchmark Evaluation
experiments.detail: Models of 0.5B, 1.5B, and 7B parameters are pretrained from scratch on web data processed by DataOrchestra; downstream performance is measured on 11 benchmarks (ARC‑E, ARC‑C, MMLU, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, PIQA, CommonsenseQA, SIQA, RACE, OpenBookQA, SciQ) using average accuracy over three recent checkpoints.

experiments.title: Baselines and Comparisons
experiments.detail: Baselines include raw data, ProX (line‑level noise removal), RePro, ReWire, and mixtures; DataOrchestra consistently outperforms them, with the 7B model achieving 40.13 average versus 38.88 for ProX.

experiments.title: Compute Savings Analysis
experiments.detail: Approximately 35% of chunks are dropped or left untouched; NP removes the most tokens, SR modestly reduces tokens, and PA increases token count, aligning with their design goals.

findings.title: Performance Gains
findings.detail: DataOrchestra yields stable average accuracy improvements across model scales, with larger models showing larger margins over baselines.

findings.title: Efficient Use of Compute
findings.detail: Skipping unnecessary cleaning stages reduces effective EFLOPs while maintaining or improving downstream quality.

findings.title: Ablation Insights
findings.detail: Removing fine‑grained plan evolution drops average accuracy from 40.13 to 39.0; omitting instruction generation further reduces it to 38.5, confirming their contribution.

contributions: Per‑example orchestration of multiple data‑processing operations
Unified framework combining NP, SR, and PA with learned decision making
Empirical demonstration of accuracy gains and compute savings across model sizes and corpora
limitations: Reliance on teacher and verifier LLMs for plan generation and verification, without quantified overhead or robustness analysis
open_questions: How does the approach scale to much larger models (e.g., >100B) and more diverse domains?
What is the impact of instruction quality on rewriting effectiveness, and can it be further optimized?
Can the verifier LLM be replaced with cheaper heuristics without sacrificing quality?

papers.title: When Derived Measurements Mislead: Quantifying and Mitigating LLM Over-Trust with Privileged-Modality Reliability Evidence
papers.abstract: Derived measurements increasingly enter large language model (LLM) pipelines as direct facts despite their instance-dependent validity. We define derived-feature over-trust (DFOT) as the failure in which a downstream LLM assigns such a measurement the epistemic status of a direct fact or uses it outside its valid scope. Using physiological sensing as a case study, D1 tests acceptance of a PPG-derived rhythm contradicted by offline ECG, whereas D2 tests rejection of an offline-confirmed reliable PPG rhythm under misleading severe history. ECG supplies training supervision and offline reference construction but is never shown to the LLM. Five estimands quantify this chain: conflict over-trust rate (COTR) and context-induced error rate (CIR) characterize D1/D2; correct repair rate (CRR) measures frozen-error repair; evidence-specific repair margin (ESRM) contrasts matched and patient-disjoint shuffled evidence; and utility harm rate (UHR) measures unnecessary verification among HIGH-reliability cases used without verification at baseline. The framework does not depend on a particular reliability generator. We demonstrate it on 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records using ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation as an illustrative baseline and PPG-only inference. On a protocol-locked 187-patient test, the baseline improves four repair and specificity endpoints by 1.82-6.69 percentage points, with all paired confidence intervals excluding zero; UHR increases by 0.67 percentage points (95% CI: -0.4 to +1.7). DFOT provides a common evaluation target for stronger mitigation methods. The code is available at https://github.com/Zongheng-Guo/When-Derived-Measurements-Mislead.
papers.comment: 25 pages, including references and supplementary material; 3 figures and 19 tables. Code: https://github.com/Zongheng-Guo/When-Derived-Measurements-Mislead

summary.evidence: 187-patient PPG-ECG tests show 1.82-6.69% improvement in repair endpoints and 0.67% UHR increase with ECG-to-PPG distillation baseline.
summary.limitations: Framework dependency on specific reliability generators and unresolved extreme low-FPR cases limit generalization.
summary.method: DFOT framework quantifies over-trust through five estimands (COTR, CIR, CRR, ESRM, UHR) using matched-vs-shuffled interventions and privileged modality evidence.
summary.problem: LLMs over-trust instance-dependent derived measurements, treating them as direct facts despite validity constraints.
summary.takeaway: DFOT defines a new evaluation target for LLM over-trust in derived measurements, with measurable mitigation via physiological case studies.
summary.why_for_you: Matches your focus on trustworthy LLMs by addressing interface-level over-trust through quantifiable physiological validation

contributions: Formal definition of DFOT as an interface-level LLM over-trust failure
Five estimands (COTR, CIR, CRR, ESRM, UHR) for quantifying derived measurement reliability
Matched-vs-shuffled interventions to distinguish instance-specific repair from generic caution

experiments.title: Baseline Models

experiments.detail: COTR, CIR, CRR, ESRM, and UHR measured across Qwen38B, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and GPT-5.5 LLMs with paired confidence intervals.
experiments.title: Metrics

findings.title: DFOT Quantification

mechanism.title: DFOT Interface Failure

mechanism.detail: ECG-derived reliability signals are distilled into PPG-only models without revealing raw ECG data, preserving modality-specific constraints.
mechanism.title: Privileged Evidence Transfer

methodology.title: Privileged Modality Distillation

methodology.detail: Controls break instance correspondence while preserving interface structure, measuring repair (CRR) and evidence specificity (ESRM) through matched (m) and shuffled (s) evidence conditions.
methodology.title: Matched-vs-Shuffled Interventions

methodology.title: Five Estimands

open_questions: How to generalize DFOT metrics beyond physiological signals to other modalities?
What are the limits of privileged modality distillation for reliability transfer?
How to balance repair rates with specificity in safety-critical applications?
deep_dive.overview: The paper formalizes DFOT as an interface-level failure where LLMs treat derived measurements as facts. It introduces a framework using physiological signals (PPG-ECG) with five estimands to quantify over-trust, validated through matched-vs-shuffled interventions. The method employs privileged modality distillation (ECG-to-PPG) to improve reliability, demonstrating measurable gains in repair rates and specificity while highlighting unresolved limitations in extreme cases.
